clinicalPearls: An inherited platelet function disorder characterised by a reduced number or content of platelet dense (delta) granules.
Dense granules store the small molecules ADP, ATP, calcium, serotonin and polyphosphate that amplify platelet activation and recruitment.
Clinically presents with lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding: easy bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia and excessive surgical or dental bleeding.
The platelet count is normal, so the disorder is a qualitative rather than quantitative defect.
Aggregometry classically shows an absent or blunted second wave with impaired response to ADP and collagen and a diminished response to arachidonic acid.
Confirmation uses whole-mount electron microscopy for dense granule count, mepacrine uptake and release by flow cytometry, or measurement of the platelet ADP:ATP ratio and secretion.
May be isolated or syndromic, occurring in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (with albinism and pulmonary fibrosis) and Chediak-Higashi syndrome (with immunodeficiency).
Treatment employs antifibrinolytics and desmopressin for minor bleeding and procedures, reserving platelet transfusion for major haemorrhage.
reference.pathophysiology: Delta storage pool deficiency arises from defective biogenesis or cargo loading of platelet dense granules, the lysosome-related organelles that store the non-protein mediators ADP, ATP, calcium, serotonin and inorganic polyphosphate. Upon activation, normal platelets secrete dense granule contents, and released ADP engages P2Y receptors to amplify aggregation and recruit further platelets, producing the second wave of aggregation. When dense granules are reduced in number or content, this positive-feedback amplification fails, so platelet activation and thrombus consolidation are impaired even though adhesion and initial shape change are intact. In syndromic forms, mutations in genes governing the biogenesis of lysosome-related organelles (as in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome) or vesicle trafficking (as in Chediak-Higashi syndrome) simultaneously affect melanosomes and other organelles, accounting for the associated albinism and immune defects.
additionalDifferentials: Antiplatelet drug or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory effect
additionalInvestigations: Light transmission platelet aggregometry with ADP, collagen, adrenaline and arachidonic acid
Whole-mount transmission electron microscopy for dense granule enumeration
Flow-cytometric mepacrine uptake and release assay
Platelet nucleotide content and ADP:ATP ratio with secretion studies
Full blood count and blood film to confirm normal platelet number
von Willebrand factor antigen and activity to exclude von Willebrand disease
Examination and testing for syndromic features (albinism, immune defects) with targeted genetics
redFlags: Major haemorrhage after surgery, trauma or childbirth
Severe menorrhagia producing symptomatic iron-deficiency anaemia
Features of Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome such as progressive pulmonary fibrosis or granulomatous colitis
Recurrent severe infections or accelerated-phase lymphohistiocytosis suggesting Chediak-Higashi syndrome
Uncontrolled bleeding despite antifibrinolytic and desmopressin therapy
reference.prognosis: Isolated delta storage pool deficiency usually causes mild to moderate lifelong bleeding with a normal life expectancy when peri-procedural precautions are observed. In syndromic disease the outlook is dominated by associated features such as pulmonary fibrosis in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome or immunodeficiency in Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
pitfalls: Overlooking a qualitative platelet defect because the platelet count is normal.
Missing an underlying syndrome by not examining for oculocutaneous albinism or a history of recurrent infection.
Misinterpreting aggregometry performed after recent aspirin or non-steroidal drug use.
Relying on a single aggregometry result, as dense granule defects can give subtle or variable patterns.
Repeated platelet transfusion causing alloimmunisation and later refractoriness.
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood, current edition
International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis guidance on inherited platelet function disorders
management: Avoid antiplatelet drugs such as aspirin and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and other agents that further impair platelet function
Antifibrinolytic therapy with tranexamic acid for mucocutaneous bleeding and to cover minor and dental procedures
Desmopressin to improve platelet function and cover bleeding episodes or surgery
Reserve platelet transfusion for major bleeding or major surgery unresponsive to other measures, using leucodepleted products
Manage menorrhagia with tranexamic acid and hormonal therapy such as the combined oral contraceptive or a levonorgestrel intrauterine system, and treat iron deficiency from chronic blood loss
Peri-procedural planning with haematology, provision of a bleeding-disorder alert card, and recombinant activated factor VII for refractory bleeding
Evaluate for syndromic association such as Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, surveil related complications including pulmonary fibrosis, and provide genetic counselling
